Where a capability is not implemented, it is documented as not implemented — so you do not design around a feature that exists only in a roadmap.

pages.title: Application Deployment
pages.description: Operate supported CloudHost247 application installs and updates with deployment status, step events, per-application configuration and recovery where supported.

hero.heading: A deployment you can inspect afterwards
hero.lede: CloudHost247 records supported application installs and updates against the services they change. Follow the deployment status and step events, then inspect the application configuration and recovery options available for that operation.

sections.heading: What happens to a supported application

items.title: Choose a published application
items.body: Select an application and version that the live marketplace marks as published. The native deployment flow uses that version’s stored manifest.

items.title: Validate the target
items.body: The worker checks the application version, target server, supported hosting type and available capacity before provisioning.

items.title: Provision and record
items.body: The deployment uses the configured image and resources, then records the operation status, step state and events against the installation.

items.title: Review the outcome
items.body: Inspect the deployment record and application logs. If a supported infrastructure step fails, the worker attempts to reverse completed steps and records the result.

items.title: It is recorded
items.body: Each operation has a durable status, step states and event history rather than disappearing with a terminal session.

items.title: Versions are explicit
items.body: Native deployments use a published application version and its stored manifest; an arbitrary repository commit is not implied.

items.title: Configuration is separate
items.body: Application environment values are managed per installation; sensitive values are encrypted in storage and omitted from API responses.

items.title: Failure is visible
items.body: A failed operation is recorded with its error and event history. The worker attempts to reverse completed infrastructure steps where it can.

items.title: Scoped per application
items.body: Installations and deployment records are linked to the application and server they operate on.

items.title: Tracked over time
items.body: The deployment history shows which supported operation ran and when.

sections.heading: Git builds and CI are separate capabilities
sections.body: The core application deployment queue does not clone arbitrary Git repositories, run build commands or execute test suites. It deploys published application versions and their configured images. Git-based builds depend on a control-panel integration that is enabled for the selected service; check the live panel catalogue before ordering. Run tests in your own CI system.

faqs.q: Can I deploy on every commit?
faqs.a: Not through the core deployment queue: it does not watch Git repositories or run CI. A configured Git-enabled control panel may provide commit-triggered deployments; otherwise use your own CI and the supported platform API where available.

faqs.q: What happens if a deployment fails?
faqs.a: The operation is recorded. The worker attempts to reverse completed infrastructure steps, but recovery of a previous application version depends on the operation and provider.
The deployment record keeps status, step states and event history. Source-build logs are available only if the selected Git-enabled panel provides them.

faqs.q: Can I use the same application in staging and production?
faqs.a: You can create separate application installations with distinct configuration and domains, subject to the services and capacity available in your account.

pages.title: Application Environments
pages.seoTitle: Environment Variables, Volumes & Per-App Domains | CloudHost247
pages.description: Configure CloudHost247 application environments: environment variables and secrets, persistent volumes, per-application domains and certificates.

hero.heading: Configuration belongs outside the code
hero.lede: Environment variables, secrets, persistent volumes and the domain the application answers on — all attached to the application rather than committed to a repository.

items.title: Environment variables
items.body: Plain configuration values injected into the process, so the same image runs in different places with different values.

items.title: Secrets
items.body: Sensitive values are stored encrypted in the platform, not shown again after saving, and never included in an API response.

items.title: Volumes
items.body: Storage declared by the application so data survives a redeploy, a rebuild or a move between hosts.

items.title: Domains
items.body: A domain can be attached to the application, with its own certificate, so environments are distinguishable at a glance.

items.title: Service connections
items.body: Reference a database or cache the account owns instead of pasting raw hostnames and ports everywhere.

items.title: Separate per environment
items.body: Staging and production are separate applications with separate configuration — the only way they can be safely different.

items.label: Never commit secrets
items.body: If a credential is in the repository, it is in every clone and every backup of that repository. Rotate it once it has been.

items.label: Keep environments structurally identical
items.body: The same services, the same variable names, different values. Divergent structure is what turns a staging pass into a false negative.

items.label: Give the environment its own domain
items.body: An address that identifies the environment prevents the classic incident of debugging production while thinking it is staging.

faqs.q: Can I change a variable without redeploying?
faqs.a: Configuration changes are applied to the application and take effect on the next release, so the running release always matches a recorded state.
Yes. Secret values are stored encrypted, are not returned to the browser after being saved, and are excluded from API responses.

faqs.q: What happens to volumes on redeploy?
faqs.a: They persist. That is the point of declaring them: the container is replaceable, the data is not.

pages.title: Node.js Hosting
pages.description: Node.js hosting on CloudHost247: review available runtimes and product integrations for process supervision, environment configuration, application logs and domains.

hero.heading: Node.js as a long-running service, not a script
hero.lede: A Node application is a process that has to stay up. The platform supervises it, restarts it when it fails, keeps its logs and routes a domain to it.

sections.heading: The operational parts of a Node app

items.title: Supervision
items.body: The process is managed and restarted after a crash, which is what turns a successful test into a running service.

items.title: Configuration
items.body: Ports, connection strings and flags supplied as environment variables rather than edited into the source.

items.title: Logs
items.body: Standard output and error are captured per application so an unhandled rejection is findable.

items.title: Deployment
items.body: Native application deployments install published versions and configured images. Git source builds depend on an enabled control-panel integration.

items.title: Data services
items.body: Managed MySQL-compatible, PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Redis services your application connects to.

items.title: Domains and certificates
items.body: Attach the hostname the service answers on, and let the certificate be issued for it.

sections.heading: Bring your own runtime discipline
sections.body: The platform supplies the process management, isolation and observability. Dependency pinning, lockfiles, dependency audits and choosing a supported Node release remain the application's responsibility — and the ones that go wrong in production are almost always there.

faqs.a: WebSocket connections terminate at the application, and the platform routes the domain to it. If your application upgrades connections, that works at the application layer.

faqs.q: Can I run a worker alongside the web process?
faqs.a: Yes. A worker is another process on the same environment, or its own application if you prefer to scale it separately.
The versions the platform is configured to provide. If you need a specific release for a dependency reason, confirm it before committing to a migration.

pages.title: PHP Hosting
pages.description: PHP hosting on CloudHost247: review available runtime versions, Composer, databases and scheduled-task support in the selected hosting product.

hero.heading: PHP that is patched, tuned and yours
hero.lede: A maintained PHP runtime with the extensions applications actually declare, plus the pieces a real PHP application needs: Composer, cron, OPcache and a database.

items.title: Maintained PHP
items.body: Runtimes that receive security updates, so an old version is a choice rather than an inheritance.

items.title: Extensions and Composer
items.body: The extension set applications declare, and Composer to resolve dependencies from the lock file.

items.title: Scheduled tasks
items.body: Cron entries for queues, imports and housekeeping, so the scheduled work a framework needs actually runs.

items.title: OPcache
items.body: Bytecode caching configured on, because it is the single cheapest performance win in PHP.

items.title: Databases
items.body: MySQL-compatible, MariaDB and PostgreSQL services alongside the application.

items.title: Deployment
items.body: Use the deployment method available on the selected hosting plan. Native application deployments install published images; source builds depend on a configured control-panel integration.

sections.heading: PHP shifts responsibility to the application

items.label: Keep the framework current
items.body: A framework that no longer receives security fixes is the most common cause of a compromised PHP site.

items.label: Vet what you install
items.body: Packages run with the application's privileges. A dependency is code you are choosing to run.

items.label: Use the lock file
items.body: Deploying without a lock file means deploying whatever the registry serves today — which is not the same thing as what you tested.

faqs.q: Can I choose the PHP version?
faqs.a: Where the platform is configured to offer more than one version, version is a per-application setting. The available versions are listed in the application environment rather than promised here.
Common extensions are pre-installed. If an application declares an extension that is not present, that is a deployment question to raise before you migrate.

faqs.q: Can I run a queue worker?
faqs.a: Yes — workers are long-running processes managed alongside the application, with cron available for scheduled work.

pages.title: Python Hosting
pages.seoTitle: Python Application Hosting — WSGI & ASGI | CloudHost247
pages.description: Host Python applications on CloudHost247: virtual environments, WSGI and ASGI applications, background workers, scheduled jobs and managed data services.

hero.heading: Python applications, properly hosted
hero.lede: Virtual environments per application, a WSGI or ASGI front end, background workers when the workload needs them, and a database that is not your problem to run.

sections.heading: What Python needs to run in production

items.title: Isolated environments
items.body: Dependencies installed per application, so two applications that disagree about a library version can coexist.

items.title: WSGI and ASGI
items.body: Serve synchronous frameworks and asynchronous ones, with TLS and routing in front of the application.

items.title: Workers
items.body: Long-running processes for queues and background work, supervised and restarted on failure.

items.title: Scheduled jobs
items.body: Cron for periodic work like synchronisation, reporting and cleanup, rather than a process that sleeps.

items.title: Data services
items.body: PostgreSQL, MySQL-compatible, MongoDB and Redis services your application connects to.

items.title: Logs and telemetry
items.body: Application output and resource use captured per service, so a slow query or a memory leak is visible.

faqs.q: Can I use a virtual environment I control?
faqs.a: Yes. Dependencies are installed into the application's own environment from its declared requirements.

faqs.q: Do you support Celery or similar workers?
faqs.a: Background workers are supported as processes on the application or as a separate application, with Redis or another broker available as a managed service.
The versions the platform is configured to provide. Confirm the version your application targets before migrating.

pages.title: Laravel Hosting
pages.seoTitle: Laravel Hosting — Queues, Scheduler, Storage | CloudHost247
pages.description: Laravel hosting on CloudHost247 with the application services a Laravel site may need: queue workers, scheduler jobs, storage and database options.

hero.heading: Laravel with the parts that usually get forgotten
hero.lede: A Laravel application that works locally needs four things in production: a queue worker, the scheduler, writable storage and a database. All four are part of the hosting.

sections.heading: The four things that break in production

items.title: Queue workers
items.body: Supervised worker processes so queued jobs are processed and re-started after a deployment or a failure.

items.title: The scheduler
items.body: A single cron entry running Laravel's scheduler, so you do not have to remember which tasks need which timing.

items.title: Writable storage
items.body: Persistent volumes for uploads and framework storage, so a redeploy does not erase user files.

items.title: Migrations
items.body: A database that can be dumped, restored and migrated with a backup taken before the change.

items.title: Environment configuration
items.body: The values in .env supplied per environment instead of living in the repository.

items.title: Logs
items.body: Application and queue output captured per service, which is where a failing job is actually visible.

items.title: Back up before migrating
items.body: Run the database backup first. A failed migration with no backup is a much worse day than a failed migration.

items.title: Release the new code
items.body: Deploy from the repository so the release is tied to a revision rather than to a folder someone edited.

items.title: Restart the workers
items.body: Queue workers must pick up new code; a supervised worker is restarted by the platform on release.

faqs.a: Redis is available as a managed service, and the database driver can also be used. Choose according to the load you expect.
Horizon is a Laravel process like any other worker; run it as the worker command where the plan's resources allow.
Attach a volume for the storage path, or use an object storage service. Leaving uploads inside a replaceable container is how user files disappear.

pages.title: Docker Hosting
pages.seoTitle: Docker Hosting — Images, Volumes, Registries | CloudHost247
pages.description: Run Docker containers on CloudHost247: pull from public or private registries, attach persistent volumes, inject configuration and route a domain with TLS.

hero.heading: If it runs in a container, it runs here
hero.lede: Build the image you want, run it on infrastructure you control, attach the volumes it needs and put a domain in front of it.

items.title: Image deployment
items.body: Run an image the platform can pull, so the tested artefact is the deployed artefact.

items.title: Private registries
items.body: Registry credentials are stored so a private image can be pulled without embedding a token in a script.

items.title: Volumes
items.body: State declared by the application lives on a volume, so replacing the container does not destroy data.

items.title: Configuration
items.body: Environment variables and secrets applied per application, not baked into the image.

items.title: Routing
items.body: Attach the hostname, let the certificate issue, and the container is on the internet the way you intended.

items.title: Observability
items.body: Logs, resource use and restart behaviour recorded, so a crash loop is something you can see.

sections.heading: Things that make containers safe to run

items.label: Pin the tag
items.body: A moving tag means a redeploy can change the application without anyone deciding to change it.

items.label: Do not run as root by default
items.body: A container that does not need root should not have it; privileged containers widen the blast radius for no benefit.

items.label: Keep state on volumes
items.body: Anything written inside the container filesystem is temporary by definition, whatever it looks like during testing.

items.label: Choose small base images
items.body: A smaller image pulls faster, starts faster and presents fewer packages to keep patched.

faqs.a: The platform runs containerised services rather than executing a compose file directly. Multi-service applications are modelled as the services the account owns.

The core deployment flow installs published application versions from configured images; it does not build arbitrary repositories. A Git-enabled control panel may support source builds when that integration is configured for your service.

faqs.q: Do you provide a container registry?
faqs.a: Registries are not operated by this platform. Use a registry you control or a public one, and supply credentials where the image is private.
